strengths: AudioX has impressive breadth, supporting text-, video-, image-, and audio-conditioned generation across sound, music, inpainting, and completion within one model.
The paper evaluates many recent baselines on several datasets and reports strong results in some settings, particularly VGGSound text-to-audio, MusicCaps text-to-music, and V2M video-to-music.
The large-scale captioning effort could be valuable to the community if the promised captions, filtering procedures, and licenses are released.
The paper includes masking, modality-combination, unified-versus-specialist, and human-evaluation experiments, and reports useful high-level training details.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited: the system largely combines a pretrained latent DiT with standard frozen CLIP, T5, and audio encoders, concatenated conditioning, and input masking. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish this from prior multimodal conditional diffusion systems.

The main comparisons are heavily confounded by training data and scale. AudioX uses target-domain VGGSound data, roughly 5.7M V2M clips, and 11.7K hours of proprietary text-music data, while baseline data, parameter counts, adaptation, and inference settings are not controlled. No data-matched or scale-matched baseline isolates gains from the architecture or masking strategy.

Claims of broadly superior performance are overstated. For example, MMAudio is substantially better on AVVP video-to-audio KL, FD, and alignment, while AudioX's image-audio alignment is 0.23 versus Im2Wav's 0.41. Several other tables similarly show mixed rather than uniformly state-of-the-art results.

The evaluation does not adequately establish multimodal integration. IS, FD, and FAD measure marginal quality rather than adherence to each condition; text-video inputs receive only one ambiguous alignment score; and no conflict, controllability, or temporal-synchronization tests are provided. Some evaluation captions are generated from the target audio itself, further limiting conclusions about independently supplied conditions.

The masking evidence is weak. Mask-ratio and unified-model analyses aggregate IS across heterogeneous tasks without uncertainty, seeds, or task-wise results; the reported input-masking improvements are modest; and training budgets and controls for feature masking and specialist models are unspecified.

Important reproduction details are missing, including token dimensions and positional encoding, conditioning injection, modality/task sampling, classifier-free dropout, mask geometry, diffusion schedule, preprocessing, split deduplication, and the inpainting preservation procedure. The promised code link is absent, and the proprietary music corpus prevents full reproduction.

The human study uses only 10 vaguely described users and 25 examples per task, with no blinding, randomization, inter-rater reliability, confidence intervals, significance tests, recruitment details, or compensation information.

The 'anything-to-audio' framing is too broad: only a small fixed set of modalities and combinations is tested, image conditioning is implemented as padded video and evaluated in one zero-shot table, and completion quality is assessed without continuity or long-term musical-coherence metrics.

Dataset quality and responsible-use issues are not addressed. There is no human validation of millions of Qwen2-Audio captions, analysis of hallucination or bias, licensing discussion for the large audio/music collections, memorization assessment, or consideration of copyright and misuse risks.

weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited. The evaluation does not convincingly isolate the proposed method from scale and data. AudioX has 2.4B parameters and is trained on a very large mixture that includes 5.7M V2M clips and 11,679 hours of proprietary music. Several central claims are overstated. On AudioCaps, AudioX leads only some metrics and trails Tango 2 or Stable Audio Open on KL, FAD, PC, PQ, and alignment. The zero-shot image result has the worst KL and much lower alignment than Im2Wav despite being described as excellent.

The metrics are insufficient for several claimed capabilities. Video-to-audio lacks a temporal synchronization metric, video-to-music lacks beat/rhythm alignment evaluation, and inpainting and completion lack boundary-continuity or long-range-coherence measures. All generated outputs are only 10 seconds, limiting the significance of the music-completion claims.

The user study is not rigorous enough to compensate for metric limitations: only 10 listeners and 25 samples per task are used, with no description of blinding, randomization, assignment, playback conditions, confidence intervals, significance tests, or inter-rater agreement. Spectrogram-only qualitative examples cannot establish perceptual quality or semantic fidelity.

The ablations aggregate Inception Score across heterogeneous tasks without clearly stating weighting or per-task results, report no multiple seeds or statistical variation, and do not identify a validation split. Reproducibility is weak. Important details are missing, including exact masking spans and replacement operations, task/data sampling weights, training duration or step count, DiT conditioning mechanism and dimensions, audio representation and sample rate, diffusion schedule and sampler, and modality-dropout procedure. The promised code/data URL is blank, and a substantial training dataset is proprietary.

Dataset integrity and ethics require substantially more discussion. Captions generated by Qwen2-Audio are used without a human quality audit; train/test disjointness and near-duplicate removal for the large V2M corpus are not documented; and there is no discussion of music licensing, creator consent, privacy, harmful audio generation, or bias. The structured caption pipeline explicitly represents categories, counts, ordering, and timestamps, addressing useful control dimensions that ordinary captions neglect.
The paper is generally clear and visually polished, and it includes ablations of caption sources, MAF components, unified training, and conditioning modalities.
weaknesses: The main architectural novelty is limited and insufficiently specified. MAF combines familiar gating, learned-query cross-attention, self-attention, and residual updates, but dimensions, equations, masks, and implementation details are omitted. There is also no parameter-matched comparison against simpler fusion alternatives.

The dataset description is internally ambiguous. IF-caps is reported as 1.268M general-audio clips, while the listed general-audio sources total roughly 261K clips; it is unclear whether augmented captions are being counted as distinct clips. The paper provides no systematic human audit of annotation accuracy, count/timestamp precision, or caption hallucination.

The central instruction-following evaluation is potentially circular: Gemini 2.5 Pro produces initial training annotations, generates T2A-bench prompts, and serves as the automated evaluator. There is no human validation of judge accuracy, inter-rater agreement, alternative judge, or sensitivity analysis, so the large reported gains may partly reflect model- or style-specific bias.

Comparisons are heavily confounded by training resources. AudioX uses a pretrained 2.4B-parameter system and millions of additional samples, including private data, but the paper does not provide data- or compute-matched specialist and unified baselines. Baseline inference settings and whether all outputs were regenerated under identical protocols are also unclear.

The ablations do not fully support the causal claims. MAF improvements are sometimes small or non-monotonic and lack repeated runs or uncertainty estimates; the caption augmentation experiment conflates annotation quality with the amount and diversity of supervision; and the claimed cross-modal regularization effect is inferred from downstream scores rather than directly isolated.

Reproducibility is weak: important details such as training steps, task/data sampling ratios, diffusion schedule, modality dropout, audio sampling configuration, and complete MAF architecture are missing. No code, model, benchmark files, or playable samples accompany the manuscript, and proprietary annotation services plus private music data further limit replication.

The human study uses only 25 prompts per task and reports averages without confidence intervals, significance tests, rater agreement, detailed randomization, or expert-selection criteria. Spectrogram-only qualitative figures cannot establish perceptual quality or semantic adherence.

Data governance and broader impacts are unaddressed despite training on 5.7M music samples and additional private material. The paper does not discuss provenance, licensing, artist consent, memorization, copyright, dataset release feasibility, or misuse. The inclusion of the AVVP test split among annotated sources also needs clarification before the claimed out-of-domain evaluation can be trusted.

The title and conclusions overstate scope: “anything-to-audio” is evaluated primarily for three conditioning modalities, and several audio-conditioned tasks receive only limited appendix evaluation. Overall, the promising scale and results do not overcome the current validity, novelty, reproducibility, and ethics gaps for a top-tier acceptance.

The empirical scope is unusually broad. The paper evaluates numerous task/dataset combinations against many strong specialist baselines using fidelity, diversity, alignment, controllability, and human-evaluation metrics.

Results are particularly convincing for text-to-audio, text-to-music, and fine-grained instruction following. AudioX obtains substantial improvements on T2A-bench and the established AudioTime test set while remaining competitive on most other tasks.
The caption-source and MAF-component ablations provide useful evidence that structured data curation and multimodal fusion both contribute beyond the pretrained backbone.

The manuscript is generally clear and reports several important implementation facts, including backbone size, trainable parameter count, optimization settings, inference configuration, and approximate compute.
weaknesses: The instruction-following comparison is not fully controlled. AudioX is explicitly trained on the AudioTime training split and extensive count/order/timestamp supervision, whereas the baselines appear to be evaluated off the shelf. Equal-data fine-tuning or a controlled architecture comparison is needed to attribute the large gains to the proposed framework rather than task-specific supervision.

T2A-bench has a serious validation and circularity concern: Gemini 2.5 Pro helps create the training annotations, generates the benchmark prompts, and serves as the audio annotator and final judge. There is no reported human validation, judge-human agreement, repeatability analysis, or comparison with an independent detector, and reliance on a proprietary changing service limits reproducibility.

Dataset documentation is insufficient for a contribution of this scale. The paper does not adequately describe provenance, licensing, consent, filtering, deduplication, or train-test leakage checks for the 5.7M video-music clips and the 175K private long-form music examples. It also provides no direct human audit of IF-caps annotation accuracy and no substantive limitations or ethics discussion concerning copyrighted music and misuse.

The architectural novelty is moderate: MAF combines familiar gating, learned-query cross-attention, and self-attention. Its ablation compares against a model with 60M fewer parameters, without a parameter-matched concatenation or standard-resampler baseline, repeated runs, or uncertainty estimates. Some component differences are very small, and full MAF is not best on the ordering metric, making claims that every component is essential too strong.

Evaluation of multimodal conditioning remains incomplete. Video tasks lack a dedicated audiovisual synchronization metric, video-to-music lacks rhythmic alignment evaluation, prompt-free Inception Score cannot establish conditional control, and inpainting is not assessed for boundary continuity or preservation of unmasked regions.

The human study uses only 25 examples per task and reports means without confidence intervals, significance tests, inter-rater agreement, assignment details, or participant/compensation protocol. More broadly, many numerical gains lack repeated-run uncertainty, and baseline inference settings are not documented sufficiently to establish strict comparability.

Reproduction would require additional details about modality/task sampling ratios, MAF dimensions and equations, conditioning dropout and classifier-free guidance, diffusion schedule, output lengths, inpainting sampling constraints, checkpoint selection, and the exact release scope. The stated future release is weakened by the dependence on private data and proprietary annotation/evaluation services.

The claimed cross-modal regularization effect is not causally isolated. Changing caption sources affects several jointly trained tasks simultaneously, and the paper provides no controlled experiment separating caption quality from data quantity, shared optimization, or task-mixture effects.

Comparison fairness is difficult to assess: baseline checkpoint selection, prompt formatting, generation duration, seeds, inference configuration, and whether results were regenerated uniformly are largely undocumented. AudioX also benefits from substantially more and partly private training data, so the tables do not isolate architectural progress.

Claims are stronger than the results warrant. Reproducibility is presently poor: code, captions, benchmark, and evaluation pipeline are only promised for future release; the main annotation and judge model is proprietary and version-dependent; and no listenable supplementary outputs are supplied, while spectrograms alone cannot substantiate perceptual-quality claims.
